opus-5.5.text:
I think it's quite possible, and in some ways I think it's where things will eventually have to go, although probably not right away.

Right now, most of the field builds on top of vision-language models. You take a pretrained VLM, attach an action head, and fine-tune on robot data. That makes a lot of sense pragmatically. Language models have absorbed an enormous amount of world knowledge, semantic understanding, and some reasoning ability, and robot data is scarce and expensive. So borrowing that backbone gives you a huge head start, especially for generalization to new objects, new instructions, and new scenes.

But I don't think language is necessarily the right foundation for physical intelligence. A lot of what a robot needs to know isn't well expressed in text. Things like how much force to use, how an object will deform, how contact evolves over a few hundred milliseconds, how to recover when something slips. Humans learn most of that before we can talk, and we learn it through interaction, not through reading. When you build on a language model, you inherit its representations, which are optimized for predicting tokens, and then you have to fight against them to get fine-grained, high-frequency, contact-rich control. So there's a real mismatch.

So the question becomes: what would a native robot training pipeline look like? I think it has a few pieces. First, a pretraining objective that's grounded in the physical world, probably something like predicting the future, video and world modeling, learning dynamics from huge amounts of video of humans and robots doing things. Second, large-scale robot interaction data, whether from teleoperation, from deployed fleets, or from simulation, so the model learns the action side and not just passive observation. And third, some form of reinforcement learning or self-improvement in the real world, where the robot gets better through its own trial and error rather than only imitating demonstrations. That last part is what language models arguably got from RLHF and reasoning RL, and robotics hasn't really had its equivalent moment at scale yet.

The main bottleneck is data. Language models had the internet. Robotics doesn't have an internet of actions. So a fully separate pipeline only becomes viable once we have a data engine that scales, and I think that's the thing people are really racing toward right now: cheaper hardware, better data collection, more robots out in the world generating experience.

Realistically, I expect a hybrid for a while. Language and vision models will still provide the high-level semantics, the "what should I do and why," while a separately trained, physically grounded model handles the "how do I actually do it with my body." Over time, as robot data grows, I'd expect the physical side to become more and more central, and maybe at some point language becomes just one input modality to a brain that is fundamentally about acting in the world, rather than the other way around.

r001.rationale: The response imagines a brain fundamentally focused on acting in the world, with language as one input modality, as a possible longer-term direction beyond the current hybrid approach.

r002.rationale: It proposes physical-world pretraining and robot interaction data for a native robot pipeline, but does not suggest including robotics in the pretraining of a unified multimodal model.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's possible, but I want to be careful about what "separate" means. The honest answer is that the field is split right now, and I'm genuinely uncertain which way it lands.

Let me lay out the two camps. One camp says the robot brain is basically a vision-language model with an action head bolted on. You take all the world knowledge and reasoning that lives inside a large language model, and you teach it to output motor commands. The appeal is obvious. Language models already understand that a cup is for holding liquid, that you shouldn't put a knife blade-first into a child's hand, that "clean up the kitchen" decomposes into a sequence of smaller tasks. Rebuilding that semantic knowledge from scratch, from robot data alone, seems wasteful and maybe impossible given how little robot data exists.

The other camp says language is the wrong substrate for control. A robot brain has to deal with continuous time, contact dynamics, latency measured in milliseconds, and sensory streams that have nothing to do with tokens. Forcing all of that through an architecture designed to predict the next word is like asking a poet to drive a forklift by describing what they see. And the data story is different too. Language models learned from a trillion-token corpus that already existed on the internet. There is no internet of robot experience. You have to generate it, through teleoperation, simulation, or the robot's own exploration. That data has a totally different shape, and it may want its own pretraining recipe.

So where do I actually sit? I think the "complete separate pipeline" vision is plausible for the lower layers of the stack. The parts that handle perception, dynamics, and fast control probably do want their own training regime, probably heavy on video prediction and world modeling, learning how physical scenes evolve rather than how sentences continue. I don't think you get good hands from a language model. You get good hands from seeing and feeling enormous amounts of physical interaction.

Where I'm skeptical of full separation is at the top of the stack. The moment the robot has to understand an instruction, infer a human's intent, or reason about an unfamiliar object, you're pulling on exactly the knowledge that language models already compressed. Throwing that away to stay architecturally pure seems like a bad trade. My guess is the realistic outcome is a hybrid, where the physical foundation model is trained largely on its own, and the language model sits on top as a planner or a translator, and the interesting engineering is the interface between them.

The thing I'd actually watch is whether the physical foundation model, once it's good enough, starts to acquire the semantic knowledge on its own. If a model trained purely on video and interaction begins to understand that cups hold water because it has watched water get poured ten million times, then the dependency on language models weakens, and the "separate brain" story becomes real. We're not there yet. But I wouldn't rule it out within a few years, and I'd rather bet on the pipeline that doesn't need to borrow its understanding of the world from text.

r001.rationale: It describes a vision-language model with an action head as an alternative that uses a language model’s knowledge to produce robot motor commands.

r002.rationale: It discusses training a robot model separately and adding an action head to a vision-language model, but does not suggest including robotics in the unified model’s pretraining.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s possible, but I’d separate two questions: whether a robot can have its own training pipeline, and whether it needs to learn everything independently of a large language model.

For the first, yes. A robot’s core learning problem is different: it has to connect perception to action and learn from the consequences. Its training pipeline could be built around observations, actions, and feedback from interacting with the world. Language doesn’t have to be the foundation of that loop.

The harder question is how you get enough useful experience. A language model learns from existing text. A robot needs experience that tells it what happens when it acts, and collecting that experience can be slow and expensive. So simulation, transferring skills between tasks, and learning safely from failures become central.

But I wouldn’t make complete separation the goal. If a language model helps the robot understand an instruction or use existing knowledge, that’s useful. The important thing is that the robot can ground that knowledge in what it perceives and what it can actually do. I can imagine an independent learning system for physical interaction, with language models contributing where they help.

r001.rationale: The response allows language models to contribute knowledge, but describes an independent physical-interaction learning system rather than a unified model combining robot control with other modalities.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest including robotics in a unified model’s pre-training; it describes learning from observations, actions, and feedback separately.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s possible, but I’d separate two questions: whether a robot needs its own training pipeline, and whether it needs to be completely independent of large language models.

A robot’s training pipeline has to address things that language training alone doesn’t cover: perception, movement, physical interaction, and the consequences of actions over time. Describing how to pick up a cup is very different from picking it up without dropping it. The robot needs feedback from interacting with the world.

But that doesn’t mean we should exclude language models. They could contribute useful capabilities, like interpreting instructions or breaking a task into steps, while a separate system learns how to execute those steps physically.

So I see a dedicated robot training pipeline as a plausible direction. Complete independence is a stronger claim. The interesting question is whether that independence produces better learning and more reliable behavior, or whether combining the two gives us a better system.

r001.rationale: The response allows combining language-model capabilities with a separate system for physical execution, but does not present a unified multimodal model that also controls the robot as an alternative.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest including robotics in a unified model’s pre-training; it describes a separate system learning physical execution.
